source: From Skidding to Rolling
A ball that starts out sliding skids until v = Rω, losing energy to kinetic friction on the way.
Students assume a thrown bowling ball rolls without slipping from the moment it lands.

Rolling Dynamics assumed rolling without slipping from the start. A bowling ball doesn't begin that way: it lands on the lane sliding, with almost no spin. Kinetic friction then works on it until it rolls.

While the ball slides, kinetic friction $\mu_kMg$ acts backward at the contact point. It slows the center, $v = v_0 - \mu_kgt$, and its torque $\mu_kMgR$ spins the ball up: for a solid ball ($I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$), $R\omega = \tfrac{5}{2}\mu_kgt$. Sliding stops when $v = R\omega$: $$v_0 - \mu_kgt = \tfrac{5}{2}\mu_kgt \;\Rightarrow\; t = \dfrac{2v_0}{7\mu_kg}, \quad v = \tfrac{5}{7}v_0.$$ A slicker route: friction acts at the contact point and gravity balances the normal force, so angular momentum about any point on the floor stays constant: $Mv_0R = MvR + I\omega$ gives the same $\tfrac{5}{7}v_0$ in one line, without $\mu_k$.

An object launched sliding with no spin skids until $v = R\omega$, then rolls at $v = \dfrac{v_0}{1 + I/(MR^2)}$: $\tfrac{5}{7}v_0$ for a solid ball, $\tfrac{2}{3}v_0$ for a disk, $\tfrac{1}{2}v_0$ for a hoop. During the skid, kinetic friction turns kinetic energy into heat; once it rolls, that stops.
A bowling ball on a lane with $\mu_k = 0.2$: the speed line and the $R\omega$ line meet at $v = 5\ \text{m/s}$, after about 1 s.
A ball lands sliding at $7\ \text{m/s}$ with no spin; $\mu_k = 0.20$. How long does it skid, how fast does it then roll, and how far does it skid?

What fraction of the ball's starting kinetic energy is lost while it skids?
Energy lost to friction
$\tfrac{2}{7}$, about 29%.
Start: $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv_0^2$. End: $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2(1 + \tfrac{2}{5}) = \tfrac{7}{10}M\left(\tfrac{5}{7}v_0\right)^2 = \tfrac{5}{14}Mv_0^2$.
Lost: $\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{5}{14} = \tfrac{2}{14} = \tfrac{1}{7}$ of $Mv_0^2$, which is $\tfrac{2}{7}$ of the starting energy.

Spin at launch changes the outcome, and the angular momentum shortcut still works. If the ball starts with angular velocity $\omega_0$ (positive in the rolling direction), then $Mv_0R + I\omega_0 = (MR^2 + I)\dfrac{v}{R}$ gives $v = \dfrac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c}$ with $c = I/(MR^2)$. Backspin ($\omega_0 < 0$) makes the final speed smaller; enough topspin can make the ball speed up as friction grips.

Assuming a thrown bowling ball rolls without slipping from the moment it lands, so it keeps its full speed and $v = R\omega$ at once. A ball can't spin up without a torque, and the only torque comes from kinetic friction while it slides. Check: at landing $R\omega = 0$ but $v = v_0$, so $v \ne R\omega$: it must skid first, and the final speed is less than $v_0$.
